newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania cbank to control money policy again - govt.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania cbank to control money policy again - govt.

text.p: Lithuania's new right-wing government on Thursday is promising to gradually restore monetary control to the central bank starting in 1998 and abolish the currency board model.

These were some of the details in a draft programme drawn up by the Baltic state's new coalition government of the Homeland Union, headed by independence hero Vytautas Landsbergis, and the right-wing Christian Democrats.
"The free-floating regime, controlled by the central bank using classical methods, will be implemented no earlier than 1998," said the programme, obtained by Reuters.

Under the current currency board system, the central bank is barred from using the traditional tools to influence monetary policy. Instead, it guarantees it will have one dollar in reserves for every four litas in circulation, freezing the exchange rate at that level.
The new government has criticised the currency board system, saying that it overvalues the litas and chokes off exports.
The government also said it would gradually cut value-added tax to 15 percent from 18 percent and give industries involved in production a ten-year break on profit tax.
In addition, the programme said "we expect to finish the second stage of state-property privatisation" and the energy sector should be "demonopolised and decentralised."
However, the only commitment the programme gave was to the sale of the state-run telecommunications company.

The government said the budget deficit for 1996 will be 1.1 billion litas, or 3.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), an increase of 400 million litas over the figure set by the out-going administration.
It predicted 1997 inflation of 15 percent and ten percent in 1998. GDP growth of eight to nine percent was expected in 1997.
